title: Trading, market structure, settlement, and the regulatory back end

reading.h: The 1934 Act back end and issuer reporting
reading.body:
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs everything after a security is issued. It makes public companies keep the market informed with regular reports. The **10-K** is annual and audited. The **10-Q** is quarterly and unaudited. The **8-K** reports a material event within **4 business days**. These are disclosure documents; the SEC reviews them for completeness and never approves the company.

The Act also created the SEC. It requires exchanges and broker-dealers to register. It sets the anti-fraud Rule 10b-5 and the net-capital and customer-protection rules (15c3-1 and 15c3-3). It gave margin authority to the Fed. Think of it as the rulebook for the ongoing life of a security and the people who trade it.

reading.h: Section 16 vs. 13D/13G vs. insider trading — three separate things
reading.body:
These three sound alike and get confused, so keep them apart. **Section 16 is insiders' paperwork and profit clawback.** Insiders are officers, directors, and owners of **more than 10%**. They file Form 3 within 10 days of becoming an insider, Form 4 within **2 business days** of a change, and Form 5. The short-swing profit rule 16(b) lets the issuer recover any profit from a purchase and sale within **6 months**, no matter the intent.

**Sections 13(d) and 13(g) are big buyers announcing themselves.** Buying more than **5%** of a class with intent to influence control triggers a **Schedule 13D**. A passive investor files the shorter **Schedule 13G**.

**Insider trading is using secrets.** Trading on material nonpublic information in breach of a duty is illegal. Intent matters, and civil penalties reach **treble (3×)** the profit gained or loss avoided, on top of criminal exposure. In one line: 16 is paperwork and a no-fault clawback, 13D is disclosure of a big stake, and insider trading is fraud.

Every sell order must be marked **long, short, or short-exempt** (Rule 200). A seller is "long" only if it owns the shares and can deliver them. Before any short sale, the broker-dealer must **locate** the shares (Rule 203). That means it borrows them, arranges to borrow them, or has a reasonable belief they can be borrowed for settlement.

**Rule 201 is the short-sale circuit breaker.** When an NMS stock drops **10%** from the prior close, a limit kicks in for the rest of that day and the next day. Short sales may then execute only at a price **above the national best bid**. A stock lands on the **threshold list** when fails reach both **10,000 shares and 0.5% of shares outstanding** for 5 straight settlement days. Short sales must be done in a margin account. The old "uptick tick test" was ended in 2007, so do not pick it.

reading.h: Market structure: NYSE, Nasdaq, OTC, and Reg NMS
reading.body:
The **NYSE** is an **auction** market. Buyers compete with buyers, and one **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** per stock runs the auctions and keeps a fair and orderly market. The DMM replaced the old "specialist." **Nasdaq** is a **dealer** market of competing **market makers** who post firm two-sided quotes. Its display levels are **Level 1** (best bid and ask), **Level 2** (every market maker's quotes), and **Level 3** (a market maker's own entry terminal).

"OTC" now means non-exchange-listed. The OTC Markets tiers are OTCQX, OTCQB, and Pink. The OTCBB stopped in 2021, so treat it as history. **Alternative trading systems (ATSs)**, which are ECNs and dark pools, register as broker-dealers under Reg ATS. **Regulation NMS** ties the markets together. **Rule 611 (order protection, or trade-through)** bars executing at a worse price than a protected quote elsewhere, and the **NBBO** is the best bid and offer across all venues.

reading.h: Order types and reading the tape
reading.body:
A **market order** guarantees execution, not price. A **limit order** guarantees price or better, not execution. A **stop order** sits idle until a print **at or through** the stop price **elects** it. It then becomes a **market order** and fills at the next price. A **stop-limit** is elected the same way but becomes a **limit order**, so in a fast market it may never fill.

Here is the placement mnemonic. Orders **below** the market are **B**uy **Li**mit and **S**ell **S**top, or "BLiSS." Orders **above** the market are **S**ell **L**imit and **B**uy **S**top, or "SLoBS."

The price drops on the ex-date, so **Rule 5330** reduces only the below-market (BLiSS) open orders by the dividend on the ex-date. It rounds down to the next lower valid tick, unless the order is marked **DNR**. Above-market orders are not adjusted. Stock splits adjust everything, and reverse splits cancel open orders.

A firm acts as **agent (broker)** or as **principal (dealer)**, never both on one trade. As agent, it matches the customer with another party and charges a disclosed **commission**. As principal, it trades from its own inventory and earns a **markup or markdown** in the price. A **riskless principal** buys only after it gets the customer's order and then resells at once. So its markup is measured off its **contemporaneous cost**, not old inventory, and for equities it must be disclosed.

**FINRA Rule 2121, the 5% policy, is a guideline, not a hard cap.** Markups must be fair and reasonable given the security type, liquidity, price, and trade size. The base is the **prevailing market (inside) price**, never the dealer's cost. **Disclosure does not cure** an excessive markup. Municipals and new issues are excluded.

**Confirmations (Rule 10b-10)** are due at or before the transaction is complete, which is settlement. Each must show the firm's capacity, the commission if it acted as agent, whether the firm is a market maker, and any payment-for-order-flow.

Regular-way settlement is **T+1** for essentially everything: stocks, corporate and municipal bonds, Treasuries, options, and funds. It moved from T+2 on May 28, 2024. **Cash settlement** is same-day. **Reg T payment** is due **T+3**, which is settlement plus 2. If a customer does not pay, the firm sells the position and freezes the account for **90 days**. Behind the scenes, DTCC units do the plumbing: **NSCC** clears and nets trades, **DTC** is the central depository, and the **OCC** issues and guarantees listed options.

Trade-reporting timing is tested hard. **TRACE** (corporate and agency bonds) and **RTRS** (munis) both require reporting within **15 minutes**. A proposed 1-minute standard was withdrawn in 2025. The **TRF** (listed stocks traded off-exchange) and **ORF** (non-listed OTC equities) require reporting within **10 seconds**.

Volatility brakes are three separate systems. Market-wide **circuit breakers** on the S&P 500 give a 15-minute halt at **−7%** or **−13%** if before 3:25 pm ET, and close the market for the day at **−20%**. Single-stock **LULD** price bands and Reg SHO Rule 201 are the other two.

Form 3 within 10 days of becoming an insider; Form 4 within 2 business days of a change; Form 5 after fiscal year-end. Short-swing profit clawback = within 6 months.

Both are elected by a print at or through the stop. A stop becomes a MARKET order (fills at next price); a stop-limit becomes a LIMIT order (may never fill in a fast market).
Below the market: Buy Limit, Sell Stop. Above the market: Sell Limit, Buy Stop.
Only below-market (BLiSS) open orders are reduced by the dividend on the ex-date, rounded down to the next valid tick, unless DNR. Above-market orders unchanged.

flashcards.front: Regular-way settlement and Reg T payment
flashcards.back: Regular way = T+1 (all products since 5/28/2024); cash = same day; Reg T payment = T+3; unpaid → 90-day freeze.
TRACE (corp/agency bonds) and RTRS (munis) = 15 minutes; TRF (listed off-exchange) and ORF (OTC equities) = 10 seconds; CAT next trading day.
−7% (L1) / −13% (L2) → 15-minute halt only if before 3:25 pm ET; −20% (L3) → market closed for the day.

flashcards.front: Agent vs. principal vs. riskless principal
flashcards.back: Agent: matches, charges commission. Principal: trades from inventory, earns markup. Riskless principal: buys only after the customer's order, markup measured off contemporaneous cost.

quiz.stem: Regular-way settlement of a corporate stock transaction occurs:
options: On the same business day as the trade
Two business days after the trade date
One business day after the trade date
Three business days after the trade date
quiz.explanation: Regular-way settlement has been T+1 (one business day after the trade) since May 28, 2024. T+2 is the pre-2024 value and a classic stale-material trap; same-day is cash settlement; T+3 is the Reg T payment date, not settlement.

quiz.stem: A customer enters an order to sell 100 XYZ at 40 STOP. After entry the tape shows: 40.25, 40.10, 40.00, 39.85, 39.95. At what price is the order executed?
quiz.explanation: The print at 40.00 is at the stop, so the order is elected and becomes a market order; it then executes at the NEXT print, 39.85. Choosing 40.00 confuses election with execution; 39.95 would be relevant only for a stop-limit at 39.90 or lower.

quiz.stem: At 1:15 pm ET the S&P 500 is down 7% from the previous close. Under the market-wide circuit-breaker rules:
options: Trading continues; a halt occurs only at a 13% decline
Trading halts for the remainder of the day
Trading in all equity markets halts for 15 minutes
Only the S&P 500 stocks are paused for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: A Level 1 (−7%) or Level 2 (−13%) breach before 3:25 pm ET triggers a 15-minute market-wide halt. Closing for the day is the Level 3 (−20%) consequence; the 5-minute single-stock pause describes LULD, a different system.

quiz.stem: An officer of a public company buys 1,000 shares in January and sells them at a $4,000 profit in April of the same year. Under Section 16(b):
options: The trade is legal because the officer held the shares for several months
The issuer may recover the $4,000 profit, regardless of the officer's intent
The SEC will impose a treble-damage penalty of $12,000 for insider trading
No consequence follows unless the officer used material nonpublic information
quiz.explanation: The short-swing profit rule lets the issuer recover any profit from a purchase and sale within 6 months, with no need to prove intent or misuse of information. Treble damages and the MNPI requirement belong to insider-trading law, which is a separate matter from the no-fault 16(b) clawback.

quiz.stem: The inside market for an OTC equity is 30.00 - 30.20. A firm with no position receives a customer order to buy 300 shares, buys 300 from a market maker at 30.20, and immediately resells them to the customer at 30.50. Under Rule 2121, the markup is:
options: Approximately 0.99%
Approximately 1.64%
Approximately 1.67%
Not measured as a percentage, because the firm acted as principal
quiz.explanation: This is a riskless principal trade, so the markup is measured off the firm's contemporaneous cost of $30.20: (30.50 − 30.20) / 30.20 = 0.99%. Measuring against the bid (30.00) gives the 1.64% trap; the point is that the base is what the firm just paid, not the inside bid or old inventory.

quiz.stem: A customer has two open GTC orders in XYZ: buy 100 at a limit of 50.00 and sell 100 at a limit of 55.00. XYZ goes ex-dividend for a $0.125 cash dividend with no DNR instruction. On the ex-date the orders are adjusted to:
options: Buy limit reduced to 49.87; sell limit unchanged
Buy limit reduced to 49.88; sell limit unchanged
Both orders reduced by $0.125
Buy limit reduced to 49.875; sell limit reduced to 54.875
quiz.explanation: Only below-market (BLiSS) orders are reduced on the ex-date; the buy limit is below the market and the sell limit above it, so only the buy limit changes. 50.00 − 0.125 = 49.875, rounded DOWN to the next valid tick = 49.87. Rounding up (49.88) or adjusting the above-market sell limit are the traps.

quiz.stem: A FINRA member internalizes a customer trade in an NYSE-listed stock away from the exchange. Within what time must it report the trade to a Trade Reporting Facility (TRF)?
options: Within 15 minutes
Within 10 seconds
By 8:00 pm the same day
By the next business day
quiz.explanation: Off-exchange trades in listed (NMS) stocks are reported to a TRF within 10 seconds of execution. The 15-minute answer is the TRACE/RTRS standard for bonds, and the next-business-day answer describes CAT order-event reporting — different facilities with different clocks.

quiz.stem: Which order qualifier requires immediate execution in whole or in part, with any unfilled portion canceled?
options: Fill-or-kill (FOK)
Immediate-or-cancel (IOC)
All-or-none (AON)
Good-till-canceled (GTC)
quiz.explanation: IOC allows partial fills and cancels the remainder immediately. FOK demands the ENTIRE order at once or nothing (no partials); AON demands the entire order but may wait; GTC concerns duration, not immediacy.
